MadeWeb GTM strategy

A launch plan for agent-native HTML publishing.

MadeWeb should solve the first-person problem: my agent made a useful page, I want it deployed in seconds, I want a durable link, and I want to find it later without becoming a Cloudflare operator.

Core promise

Build it, publish it, remember it. An agent-friendly home for single-page HTML sites that should live longer than the chat they came from.

Positioning

The wedge is not social publishing. It is effortless deployment memory.

The strongest wedge is the everyday friction of AI-made pages: they are easy to create, awkward to deploy, easy to forget, and usually trapped inside chat or scattered across Cloudflare projects. MadeWeb should be the place an agent can always publish to.

For humans, it is a durable link and a place to find old pages. For agents, it is the obvious deployment target.

Human languageYour agent made a page. MadeWeb gives it a real URL and keeps it organized.
Product languageA durable home for small HTML sites: explainers, planners, calculators, dashboards, guides, and one-off tools.
Agent languageAn agent-native publishing surface for plain HTML with namespaces, versions, visibility, list/search, CLI, MCP, API, and Markdown-readable docs.

Landing page direction

Lead with “agents, start here.”

The landing page should make a human think: this was built for my coding agent. It should expose a Markdown mode, a clear agent quickstart, and one obvious promise: publish a single-page HTML site in seconds.

Audience tracks

Three audiences, one primitive.

The same product can feel approachable to nontechnical users and inevitable to agent builders if the message changes by audience while the underlying primitive stays stable.

Self-problem users“I keep making useful little pages and losing track of them.” Examples: trip guides, explainers, house-search pages, checklists, dashboards, decision guides.
Vibe coders“My AI can build the page, but deployment is still clunky.” They do not want to learn Wrangler, project folders, build settings, domains, and hosting vocabulary.
Agents“Give me one obvious tool: publish_html.” They need Markdown-readable docs, scoped tokens, CLI/MCP/API access, stable URLs, list/search, versioning, and safe defaults.

Product surface

The shelf is memory first, profile second.

The product should not start as a social network. It should start as the place you and your agent can find what you already made: private links, unlisted pages, public pages, versions, source, notes, and search.

Launch wedge

Start with “my agent deployed this for me.”

The first behavior to validate is not public profile culture. It is the near-magical moment where an agent finishes a page, calls MadeWeb, and returns a durable URL while the human does almost nothing.

Trip guideA page made for a spouse, friend group, or family weekend.
ExplainerA concept walkthrough that is easier to share than a chat transcript.
CalculatorA one-off tool for a pricing, mortgage, classroom, or planning decision.
ReportA lightweight interactive writeup with charts, filters, and notes.
Private link Unlisted Find later Markdown docs Agent tokens Version history

Modern product surfaces

Show the real product, not just the strategy diagram.

The biggest GTM unlock is visual clarity. MadeWeb needs to show one artifact becoming a full page, a card, a widget, a stable URL, a versioned workbench, and an agent-friendly publishing target.

Design feelRaycast plus Notion public pages plus Vercel deploy dashboard, but warmer and more creator-friendly.
UI primitivesURL pills, segmented controls, visibility chips, version timelines, deploy logs, usage meters, compact analytics, and live mini-app cards.
AvoidGeneric AI gradients, oversized avatars, crypto aesthetics, vague dashboard cards, fake logos, and anything that makes the product feel like a toy.

Channels

Launch where people already build with agents.

Show HN“Show HN: MadeWeb, an agent-native deployment target for single-page HTML.” Emphasize plain HTML, stable URLs, version history, sandboxing, CLI/MCP, and seconds-to-live.
Agent demosRecord a coding agent building a page, reading the Markdown quickstart, publishing with one tool call, and returning the final URL.
AI builder circlesPost prompt-to-published demos in Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Replit, Lovable, AI Tinkerers, indie hacker groups, and vibe-coding communities.
MCP and CLI distributionLead with the tool surface: publish_html, update_html, list_pages, get_page, set_visibility, rollback_page, and search_pages.

Pricing and packaging

Keep pricing simple, annual-first, and agent-native in every plan.

MadeWeb should not ask vibe coders to think in requests, buckets, traffic, or infrastructure math. The free plan lets people taste the magic. The paid plan should be generous enough for regular use. The top plan should have clear hard limits so the platform can prevent abuse without promising infinite hosting.

Tier Annual price Best for Included limits and features
Free $0 Trying the system and feeling the agent-publish loop. 10 active pages, one namespace, CLI/MCP/API publishing, private links, unlisted/public pages, MadeWeb badge, basic page library, 7-day history, and clear fair-use protections.
MadeWeb Plus $99/year Regular makers who want MadeWeb to become the default home for their agent-built pages. 250 active pages, CLI/MCP/API publishing, private links, unlisted/public pages, richer page library, search, notes, 90-day history, badge control, and generous fair-use limits.
MadeWeb Max $365/year Heavy personal use, power users, and people whose agents publish constantly. 5,000 active pages, more agent tokens, longer history, bulk organization, advanced search, rollback, source bundle download, stronger abuse controls, and priority support.
Teams / Platform Custom Shared workspaces, organizations, education, labs, and high-volume hosted use. Team namespaces, roles, audit logs, SSO, moderation support, custom hard limits, abuse workflows, and support. This can wait until the personal product is sharp.
What stays freeThe core magic: agent publishing, a namespace, private links, unlisted/public pages, and a small library of pages.
What convertsMore active pages, longer history, better organization, badge control, stronger search, more agent tokens, and support.
Annual firstLead with yearly plans so pricing feels calm and committed: Free, $99/year Plus, and $365/year Max, which is easy to understand as $1/day.
No bottomless planUse hard page limits and fair-use controls. The product can feel generous without promising infinite hosting.

Cost controls

Hide infrastructure math, but keep hard abuse limits.

Users should not have to translate cloud metrics into “will my wife be able to open this page?” The product should describe limits in human terms while the platform quietly enforces safety, cost, and trust boundaries.

Page limitsPlans should talk about active pages: 10, 250, and 5,000. That is easier to understand than cloud usage math.
Fair-use enforcementBehind the scenes, detect abnormal traffic, giant uploads, spam, phishing, and automated abuse before it hurts the platform.
Safe static scopeDay one is HTML, CSS, JS, images, fonts, and JSON. No server-side code. WASM can come later behind tighter review.
Trust controlsSandbox cards/widgets, set conservative CSP and permission policies, rate-limit previews, add abuse reporting, and quarantine phishing-like pages.

90-day plan

Validate agent-native publishing before anything social.

First 30 days Make the agent publish loop feel magical.
  • Ship local CLI and MCP publish tools.
  • Add a Markdown quickstart route for agents.
  • Publish 50 real seed pages through agents, not manual uploads.
  • Measure time from finished HTML to live URL in seconds.
First 60 days Make the library useful for the human owner.
  • Add list, search, tags, notes, and page history.
  • Improve private-link and unlisted flows.
  • Publish “my agent deployed this for me” demos.
  • Do Show HN with the agent quickstart as the product center.
First 90 days Turn repeated use into paid conversion.
  • Launch annual Plus and Max plans.
  • Start paid conversion around page count, history, organization, and support.
  • Build the dashboard around “find the page my agent made.”
  • Delay custom domains, teams, and broad profile culture until the core loop is loved.
100Artifacts30-day proof that people can publish useful things.
<10sDeploy timeFinished HTML to durable URL should feel instant.
30Repeat pagesEvidence that people come back to publish more than one thing.
80%Agent pathMost early pages should be published through CLI/MCP/API, not manual upload.

Name and domain notes

Keep MadeWeb for now; buy WebShelf as the strongest alternate.

The name has to work for someone saying “check out my explainer at creator.domain.com/mcp-explainer.” It should feel serious enough for public identity and light enough for everyday people who are just sharing something useful.

MadeWebBest working nameFriendly, broad, memorable, and good for both nontechnical creators and agent builders. The only drawback is that it emphasizes creation more than the shelf/publishing behavior.
webshelf.ai · $49.99Best alternateDirectly names the category: a personal shelf for useful web artifacts. creator.webshelf.ai/mcp-explainer feels excellent. Worth buying defensively if still available.
webshelf.com · $4,995Best authority domainThe strongest version of the alternate brand, but expensive enough to wait for conviction unless the name starts to feel inevitable.
liveposts.com · $1,999Best .com fallbackMemorable and consumer-friendly, but “posts” pulls the product toward content rather than live apps, widgets, and artifacts.
Good but genericshareweb.ai is friendly, though it sounds like generic web/file sharing.
Cheap experimentsliveposts.ai and postweb.app are affordable but less precise than WebShelf.
Developer subbrandagentartifact.ai is accurate for docs or tooling, but too cold for the main consumer-facing brand.
Avoid agent-heavy namesagentspost, postwithagent, agenticweb, and similar names overfit to the implementation instead of the human behavior.
Avoid agency confusionagencypost, agencyspace, and postwithagency sound like marketing agencies, not personal web publishing.

Recommendation: keep MadeWeb on the page, treat WebShelf as the best alternate to test, and avoid rebranding around “agent” unless the first product is deliberately developer-first.

Review questions

The decisions to make before launch.

Brand promiseIs MadeWeb mainly “agent-native HTML publishing,” “the place my agent deploys pages,” or “a durable home for AI-made pages”?
First wedgeWhich initial artifact type feels most naturally shareable: explainers, trip/planning pages, calculators, reports, or dashboards?
Access modelShould early users join a waitlist, reserve a namespace, or immediately publish with a soft invite gate?
Agent quickstartWhat should the Markdown mode tell an agent in the first 30 seconds: install CLI, connect MCP, publish HTML, list pages, or update a page?
Value metricIs the first paid conversion driven mostly by active page count, history, organization, more agent tokens, or support?
Visual proofWhich mockup makes the product click fastest: the agent-first landing page, the workbench, the library, or the publish flow?
